stories.headline: Update: Russia Kills Five in Strikes Across Ukraine; Kyiv Launches Massive Drone Assault on Moscow
stories.summary:
At least five people were killed and more than ten injured across Ukraine as Russia launched a fresh wave of aerial attacks Saturday, striking 13 regions with ballistic missiles, guided aerial bombs, and drones. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said civilian infrastructure was targeted, including a book market in Kyiv's Pochayna district and a steel plant in Kryvyi Rih, where one man was found dead in rubble. Two people in their 60s were killed when a house was destroyed in Zaporizhzhia, and another person died in Sumy.

In a significant escalatory exchange, Ukraine launched approximately 600 drones toward Moscow overnight, according to the city's mayor. A warehouse belonging to Russian online retailer Wildberries was struck and caught fire near the capital. Russia's defense ministry said 822 Ukrainian drones were intercepted, but at least seven people died across Russian regions from the strikes.

Russia claimed its attacks on Kyiv targeted a facility producing parts for Ukrainian Flamingo missiles and a drone component factory. Moscow also said it struck a steelworks in Kryvyi Rih it described as a weapons manufacturing site and hit a cargo vessel near Odesa it claimed was carrying military equipment. Ukraine has been stepping up attacks on Russian logistics hubs in recent weeks to disrupt military supplies.

A separate development drew international concern as a Ukrainian drone was reported downed in Romania, the latest in a series of drone incursion incidents in NATO airspace — raising questions about spillover risk as both sides dramatically escalate the tempo and scale of long-range strikes.

stories.headline: Update: Senate Panel Votes to Hold Fauci in Contempt After He Invokes Fifth Amendment 111 Times; Refuses Second Hearing
stories.summary:
A Senate committee voted along party lines last week to hold former NIAID Director Dr. Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress after he invoked the Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination 111 times during a July 29 hearing before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. On Friday, Fauci declined a separate request to appear before Sen. Ron Johnson's Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, with his attorney arguing a second compelled appearance would amount to politically motivated harassment.

Committee chairman Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) is seeking to send the contempt referral directly to the U.S. Attorney's Office in Washington, D.C., bypassing a full Senate vote. At the legal center of the dispute is whether Fauci can validly invoke the Fifth Amendment given that former President Joe Biden issued him a preemptive pardon before leaving office. Paul has argued the pardon eliminates Fauci's risk of federal prosecution and therefore eliminates the constitutional basis for his refusal to answer questions; Fauci's attorneys dispute that interpretation.

Republicans on the committee are investigating Fauci's role in the federal government's COVID-19 response, including the safety and efficacy of vaccines, and allegations that he funded research that may have contributed to a lab leak of the virus in China — claims Fauci has repeatedly denied. The HHS has been ordered to hand over work iPhone records, and state-level subpoenas have been issued by officials in Florida, Alabama, and Louisiana following the contempt vote.

Democrats and Fauci's supporters have characterized the investigation as a politically driven witch hunt against a public health official who spent decades in government service. The contempt referral, if acted upon by the Justice Department, could set a significant legal precedent regarding the interplay between presidential pardons and congressional oversight powers.

stories.headline: Taliban Marks Five Years in Power at Loya Jirga as UN Warns of Grave Human Rights Crisis
stories.summary:
Taliban rulers and thousands of delegates gathered at Afghanistan's traditional Loya Jirga assembly hall in Kabul on Saturday to celebrate the fifth anniversary of their return to power following the U.S. and NATO withdrawal on August 15, 2021. Senior officials delivered speeches framing Taliban rule as Afghanistan's liberation from foreign occupation, with Deputy Prime Minister Abdul Salam Hanafi declaring an end to external interventions and internal strife. Some foreign representatives attended the ceremony alongside ordinary citizens.

A top United Nations official issued a stark counter-narrative, warning of a grave and worsening human rights crisis in the country. Since seizing power, the Taliban has banned girls from attending school beyond the sixth grade, prohibited women from universities, barred women from public spaces including gyms and parks, and restricted women from traveling without a male guardian — reversing pledges made before the takeover that women would have access to education, employment, and public life.

The five-year milestone comes as international recognition of the Taliban government remains essentially nonexistent, with no country having formally recognized the administration. Taliban officials detained six staff members of an Afghan women's rights group and several UN employees earlier in August, drawing international condemnation. The anniversary underscores the enduring consequences of the 2021 withdrawal, which triggered chaotic scenes at Kabul's airport as tens of thousands of Afghans attempted to flee.

stories.headline: Update: Alaska Senate Race Tightens as Peltola Distances Herself from Harris Endorsement
stories.summary:
Alaska's U.S. Senate race is emerging as an unexpected competitive contest heading into the November midterms, with Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan facing a serious challenge from former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola. Polls remain inconclusive, but the race has drawn national attention as one of the few competitive seats in a state that typically votes reliably Republican in federal elections.

The contest became more complicated this week after former Vice President Kamala Harris sent an unsolicited fundraising email on Peltola's behalf, with half of the proceeds directed to Harris's own political organization. Peltola publicly rejected Harris's support, a calculated move in a state where Harris lost by 13 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election. The episode highlights the challenge Democrats face in red-leaning states, where national party figures can be liabilities rather than assets for down-ballot candidates.

Republicans are watching the race closely as they seek to protect their Senate majority, while Democrats see Peltola — who previously held Alaska's at-large House seat — as one of their strongest candidates in a difficult environment. The race is seen as a bellwether for whether Democrats can compete in traditionally Republican territory by running candidates who actively distance themselves from national party leadership.
